title: Packet Quest
subtitle: How the internet works, one island at a time

paragraphs: Byte is a tiny packet of data with one job: get from your laptop to a server on the other side of the world and bring a web page back. Byte has no idea how.
You're Byte's guide. Visit 25 islands, each a short lesson with a different kind of challenge, and by the end you'll both know how a click becomes a page.
steps: Press **Walk me there** at the bottom of the screen, or walk yourself with WASD or the arrow keys. Grab the coins on the causeways.
Every island has a different challenge: sort things, light beacons, step on pads in order, guess a number, match pairs and more.
Each wrong try costs a coin. Getting it right first time earns 3 stars. Finish every island to unlock the final exam in the middle.
intro.note: Numbers are typical, rounded values meant for beginners, not precise measurements.

islands.name: Many Roads Grove
islands.lead: When a web page travels to you, it is chopped into small packets. Each packet can take a different road through the network, and they are put back together at the end.
body: Byte sent seven packets to the same server. Each glowing letter is the road one packet took: **N** for the north cable, **S** for the south cable, **E** for the east cable.

activity.prompt: Walk into all 7 glowing letters to see which road most packets took.
activity.resultNote: The others went a different way and still arrived. No single road has to work for the page to load.

quiz.question: Why can packets from one page take different roads?

options.text: Because every packet is routed on its own and reassembled at the end
Because the page is sent several times by mistake
options.why: Nothing is sent by mistake. One page, many packets, many roads.

islands.remember: A page is split into packets. Each packet finds its own way and they are reassembled at the end.

islands.name: Cable Canyon
islands.lead: Data travels over three kinds of link: glass fibre, copper wire, and radio to a satellite. Each has a different delay.
body: The pairs of columns show how long a round trip takes. Grey is a short hop in the same city; colour is a long hop across an ocean.

activity.prompt: Find the slowest link for a long trip and stand on its pad, then press **Choose this one**.

options.label: Fibre
options.hint: Fibre is the fast one: light in glass crosses an ocean in a few hundredths of a second.

options.label: Copper
options.hint: Copper is slower than fibre, but a satellite round trip is far longer.

findings.caption: Round-trip delay, scaled so the longest is 100
findings.text: A satellite in high orbit is about 36,000 km up, so even light takes a long time to get there and back.

islands.remember: Fibre is fastest. A high satellite is slowest because the signal has to climb 36,000 km and come back.

islands.name: Page Load Tower
islands.lead: What happens between pressing Enter and seeing a page? Climb the tower one step at a time.

frames: Your computer asks a **DNS** server: what number is example.com? It answers with an **IP address**, like a phone number.
Your computer opens a connection to that address with a quick handshake, so both sides know the other is listening.
It sends an **HTTP request**: "please send me the page".
The server replies with the page in packets. Your browser reassembles them and draws the page.
activity.caption: Five steps, usually in well under a second.

quiz.question: What does the DNS step give your computer?

options.why: The page comes later, in the HTTP reply. DNS only answers with a number.

options.text: The IP address of the server

options.why: DNS does not change the cables. It translates a name into an address.

islands.remember: Name lookup, connect, request, reply, draw. That's a page load.

islands.name: Hop Arena
islands.lead: Byte does not fly straight to the server. It hops from router to router, and every hop adds a little delay.

activity.title: Try it: hops and delay
activity.caption: The cubes in the ring outside are the routers Byte passes. More hops, or slower hops, mean a longer wait.

quiz.question: Which journey is slower: 4 hops at 10 ms each, or 8 hops at 5 ms each?

options.why: 4 × 10 = 40 ms, and 8 × 5 is also 40 ms. Try the controls again.
8 × 5 = 40 ms, the same as 4 × 10.

islands.remember: Delay adds up hop by hop: hops × delay per hop.

islands.name: Light Speed Clock
islands.lead: Nothing beats the speed of light, and yet a request still takes noticeable time. Watch the race.

bars.label: Light in fibre, London to New York, one way
A real request there and back
The same request via a high satellite

activity.caption: Light in glass travels at about two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum. The real request is slower still because it has to go there and back and pass through routers.

quiz.question: Why is a real request slower than light itself?

options.text: It has to travel there and back, and pass through routers on the way
Because the internet uses sound instead of light
options.why: Fibre carries light pulses. The extra time is the round trip and the routers.

islands.remember: Even at light speed, a round trip across an ocean takes tens of milliseconds.

islands.name: Web or Net Hall
islands.lead: People say "the internet" and "the web" as if they were the same. They are not. The internet is the network of networks; the web is one service that runs on top of it, alongside email, video calls and games.

activity.statement: The internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.
activity.why: The internet is the global network. The web is one of many things that run on it, next to email, video calls and online games.

islands.remember: The internet carries everything. The web is just one passenger.

islands.name: Protocol Workshop
islands.lead: A protocol is a set of rules two computers agree on so they understand each other, like both speaking the same language with the same manners.

options.why: Chrome is a browser, a program that uses protocols.
A cable is hardware. Protocols are rules, not things.

islands.remember: TCP, IP and HTTP are protocols: agreed rules. Browsers and cables are not.

islands.name: Sequence Shore
islands.lead: Byte keeps forgetting what happens first. Help by putting the steps of a page load in the right order.

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps from first to last.

items.text: You type the address and press Enter
DNS turns the name into an IP address
items.note: Like looking up a phone number.

items.text: A connection is opened with a handshake
The browser sends an HTTP request
The page arrives in packets and is drawn
items.note: The last step is on your screen.

islands.remember: Type, look up, connect, request, receive. Always in that order.

islands.name: Layer Lagoon
islands.lead: The internet is built in layers. Each layer has one job and trusts the layers below it to do theirs.

activity.prompt: Match each name to its job.

pairs.right: Asks for and sends web pages

islands.remember: IP addresses, TCP delivers, DNS names, HTTP asks, TLS locks.

islands.name: Sorting Sands
islands.lead: Everything in networking is either a physical thing, a program, or a set of rules. Sorting them helps the words stop blurring together.

activity.prompt: Put each item in the right bucket.

islands.remember: Hardware you can touch, software you can run, protocols you agree on.

islands.name: Latency Ladder
islands.lead: Latency is the waiting time before an answer starts to arrive. Distance is the biggest reason it grows.

activity.prompt: Rank these round trips from fastest (top) to slowest (bottom).
activity.caption: Typical values. The bars are scaled so the satellite is 100.

islands.remember: Closer servers answer sooner. That's why big sites keep copies near you.

islands.name: Gap Grotto
islands.lead: Say it in one sentence: how does a name become a connection?

activity.text: A ___ server translates a name like example.com into an ___ address, and then your computer opens a ___ connection to it.

islands.remember: DNS gives the IP address; TCP opens the connection.

islands.name: Estimate Isle
islands.lead: Light is slower in glass than in empty space, because it keeps bouncing off the atoms of the fibre.

activity.question: Light in a fibre cable travels at roughly what percentage of its speed in a vacuum?
activity.reveal: About two-thirds. That is why a signal across the Atlantic takes around 28 ms rather than 19.

islands.remember: Light in fibre runs at about two-thirds of its top speed.

islands.name: Odd One Outcrop
islands.lead: Routers, switches and modems are boxes that move data. One of these four is not a box at all.

activity.prompt: Which one does not belong with the others?
activity.why: A browser is software on your computer. The other three are pieces of network hardware.

islands.remember: Routers, switches and modems are hardware. A browser is a program.

islands.name: Home Network Hub
islands.lead: At home, one small box does a lot: it hands out local addresses to every device, and passes traffic between your home and the wider internet.

activity.prompt: Click the part of a home network that gives your devices their local addresses.

parts.label: Modem
parts.hint: The modem talks to your provider's line. It does not hand out addresses in your home.

parts.label: Laptop
parts.hint: The laptop receives an address; it does not give them out.

parts.label: Phone
parts.hint: The phone asks for an address like any other device.

islands.remember: The home router hands out local addresses and connects your home to the internet.

islands.name: Fork in the Fibre
islands.lead: A router receives Byte and sees that the direct link ahead is jammed with traffic. Routers are allowed to choose another way.

activity.prompt: The direct road is congested. Which way should Byte go?

paths.label: Wait in line
paths.hint: Waiting adds delay and the queue may overflow. Routers prefer another route.

paths.label: Give up
paths.hint: A dropped packet has to be re-sent, which is the slowest option of all.

islands.remember: When a link is congested, routers send packets around it. The internet routes around trouble.

islands.name: Beacon Bay
islands.lead: An IP address is a number that identifies a device on a network. The old kind has four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots; the new kind is longer and uses letters and colons.

activity.prompt: Light every beacon that shows a real IP address. Leave the others dark.

islands.remember: IPv4 looks like 192.168.0.1 with numbers up to 255. IPv6 looks like 2001:db8::1. Names and http:// are not addresses.

islands.name: Handshake Steps
islands.lead: Before two computers talk over TCP, they shake hands in three quick messages, then the data flows.

activity.prompt: Step on the pads in the order of a TCP connection: the three handshake messages, then the data.

islands.remember: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, then data. Three steps to say hello.

islands.name: Address Atoll
islands.lead: Some IP addresses are **private**: they only work inside a home or office and are reused by millions of networks. Others are **public** and unique on the whole internet.
body: Private ranges start with 10., 172.16. to 172.31., or 192.168.

activity.prompt: Pick up each address orb and drop it in the right bin.

islands.remember: 10., 172.16–31. and 192.168. are private. Everything else is public and unique.

islands.name: Then and Now Point
islands.lead: Web pages have grown enormously. A page from the 1990s was a few words and a picture; a page today pulls in scripts, fonts, videos and trackers from dozens of places.

before.text: A typical page: some text, a small picture, loaded over a dial-up modem.

after.label: Today
after.text: A typical page: scripts, fonts, images and video, often from many servers.

activity.caption: Rough typical values. Today's page is about fifty times bigger.

quiz.question: Why can a modern page feel slow even on a fast connection?

options.text: It makes dozens of separate requests, each with its own waiting time
Modern text is heavier than old text
options.why: Text is tiny. The weight is in scripts, images, fonts and video, and in the number of requests.

islands.remember: Many requests mean many waits. Fewer, smaller requests make a faster page.

islands.name: Time Budget Beach
islands.lead: Where does the time go when a page loads? Guess first, then see a typical split.

activity.prompt: Set each bar to your guess of how much of the wait each step takes, then reveal the typical split.

items.label: Waiting for the server to answer

activity.revealText: Typical split for a simple page. Downloading and drawing take the biggest share, but the three waits before it add up to more than half.

quiz.question: Before any of the page arrives, roughly how much of the total time has already passed?

options.why: Look at the bars: DNS, connecting and waiting for the server happen before the first byte arrives.

islands.remember: More than half of a page load can be waiting before the first byte arrives.

islands.name: Lock Switch Station
islands.lead: Who can read what you send? It depends on which protections are switched on. Flip the switches and watch the status lamp.

readout.text: Anyone on this Wi-Fi can read what you send.
Your network provider can read what you send.
Your content is private. The network still sees which sites you visit.
Content is private, and the network only sees your VPN.

activity.caption: HTTPS protects the content. A VPN also hides which sites you visit from the local network.

quiz.question: With HTTPS on and no VPN, what can the coffee-shop Wi-Fi still see?

options.why: HTTPS encrypts the content, passwords included.
The addresses you connect to are still visible without a VPN.

islands.remember: HTTPS hides the content. A VPN also hides which sites you visit from the local network.

islands.name: Cable Cut Crystal
islands.lead: Ships' anchors cut undersea cables many times a year. What happens to your video call when one is cut?

activity.question: Predict: a major undersea cable is cut. What happens?

options.text: The internet stops for everyone nearby
options.why: The internet was designed with many paths so that no single cable is essential.

options.text: Traffic re-routes with a small delay

options.why: Email is not special; every service shares the same cables.

frames: An anchor drags across the sea floor and snaps the cable.
Routers on both ends notice that the link is dead within seconds.
They tell their neighbours, and traffic shifts to the remaining cables.
Your video stutters for a moment, then continues along a longer road.
activity.result: Traffic re-routed within seconds, with slightly more delay until the cable is repaired.

islands.remember: The internet was built to route around damage. Lose a cable and traffic finds another road.

islands.name: Padlock Pier
islands.lead: That little padlock in the address bar, and the extra letter in https, mean one thing. How sure are you what it is?

activity.question: What does the "s" in https stand for?

options.why: HTTPS can actually be a touch slower to set up, because of the extra encryption handshake.
Every website has a server; the s is about protection, not the machine.

activity.okText: Secure: the connection is encrypted with TLS.

islands.remember: https = HTTP + Secure. The padlock means the conversation is encrypted.

islands.name: Word Deck Dunes
islands.lead: The last island is a deck of cards with the words from the whole journey. Flip through them, then answer one question.

activity.prompt: Flip each card to see what the word means.

cards.back: A small chunk of data with an address on it. Pages are sent as many packets.
The number that identifies a device on a network, like a phone number.
The service that turns names like example.com into IP addresses.
The rules that deliver packets reliably and in order.
The rules browsers and servers use to ask for and send pages.
A box that reads each packet's address and sends it one hop closer.

quiz.question: Which word means a small chunk of data with an address on it?

options.why: A router is the box that forwards the chunks.
DNS turns names into addresses; it is a service, not a chunk of data.

islands.remember: Packet, IP address, DNS, TCP, HTTP, router: six words that explain most of the internet.

finale.name: The Great Upload
finale.lead: Byte is ready for the trip. For each situation, pick what really happens on the internet.

questions.question: You type a web address. What is the very first thing your computer needs to find out?

options.text: The server's IP address, using DNS

options.why: Pictures come last. First the name has to become a number.
No password is needed just to find a server.

questions.okText: Correct! Name first, then number, then connection.

questions.question: A cable between two cities is cut. What happens to packets that used it?

options.why: Routers re-route traffic; lost packets are re-sent.

options.text: They are routed around the break

questions.okText: Correct! The internet routes around damage.

questions.question: You are on café Wi-Fi with HTTPS but no VPN. What is protected?

options.text: The content of what you send and receive

options.why: HTTPS encrypts the content.
Without a VPN the addresses are still visible.

questions.okText: Correct! HTTPS locks the content; a VPN would also hide the addresses.

questions.question: Which server will usually answer fastest?

options.text: The one on the other side of the world
options.why: Distance adds delay at every hop.

options.text: The one in your own city

options.why: A high satellite is the slowest road of all.

questions.okText: Correct! Nearer servers mean lower latency.

report.heading: Byte made it!

tiers.perfect: Every challenge right on the first try. Byte could not have asked for a better guide.
tiers.great: Almost perfect. Byte is proud to have travelled with you.
tiers.pass: You got Byte home! Play again to earn more stars.

lessons: Pages travel as packets that each find their own road.
DNS turns names into IP addresses; TCP opens a reliable connection; HTTP asks for the page.
Delay adds up hop by hop, and distance is the biggest cause.
Fibre is fastest; a high satellite is slowest.
The internet is the network; the web is one service on it.
Private addresses (10., 172.16–31., 192.168.) are reused everywhere; public ones are unique.
HTTPS protects content; a VPN also hides which sites you visit.
The internet routes around damage, cut cables included.
Modern pages are slow mostly because they make many requests.
